claim: PIEZO1 is a mechanically-gated ion channel.
source: Here, we found that the mechanically-gated ion channel PIEZO1 is a key keratinocyte mechanotransducer.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established property of PIEZO1.

claim: PIEZO1 is a key keratinocyte mechanotransducer.
source: Here, we found that the mechanically-gated ion channel PIEZO1 is a key keratinocyte mechanotransducer.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches including calcium imaging, patch clamp, and behavioral assays.

claim: Keratinocyte expression of PIEZO1 is critical for normal sensory afferent firing in response to mechanical stimuli in mice.
source: Keratinocyte expression of PIEZO1 is critical for normal sensory afferent firing and behavioral responses to mechanical stimuli in mice.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo tibial nerve recordings showing decreased Aδ fiber firing in PIEZO1cKO mice.

claim: Keratinocyte expression of PIEZO1 is critical for normal behavioral responses to mechanical stimuli in mice.
source: Keratinocyte expression of PIEZO1 is critical for normal sensory afferent firing and behavioral responses to mechanical stimuli in mice.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays showing decreased mechanical sensitivity in PIEZO1cKO mice.

claim: Merkel cells and Meissner corpuscles encode unique aspects of gentle touch by tuning the responses of Aβ sensory neurons.
source: Merkel cells and Meissner corpuscles encode unique aspects of gentle touch by tuning the responses of Aβ sensory neurons, and specialized terminal Schwann cells modulate the firing of nociceptors to noxious touch (Maksimovic et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2014; Hoffman et al., 2018; Abdo et al., 2019; Ojeda-Alonso et al., 2022; Neubarth et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Keratinocytes constitute >95% of the cells in the epidermis.
source: Keratinocytes, which constitute >95% of the cells in the epidermis, are innately sensitive to mechanical force, are capable of releasing a wide array of neuroactive factors, and form close 'synapse-like' connections with intraepidermal nerve fibers (Fuchs, 1995; Koizumi et al., 2004; Tsutsumi et al., 2009; Goto et al., 2010; Lumpkin and Caterina, 2007; Hou et al., 2011; Shi et al., 2013; Barr et al., 2013; Talagas et al., 2020a; Talagas et al., 2020c).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact with supporting citations.

claim: PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 are mechanically gated, non-selective cation channels.
source: PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 are mechanically gated, non-selective cation channels that share approximately 42% amino acid similarity and are widely expressed in tissues that respond to mechanical force (e.g. lung, skin, bladder, and vasculature) (Li et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014a; Friedrich et al., 2019; Dalghi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 share approximately 42% amino acid similarity.
source: PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 are mechanically gated, non-selective cation channels that share approximately 42% amino acid similarity and are widely expressed in tissues that respond to mechanical force (e.g. lung, skin, bladder, and vasculature) (Li et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014a; Friedrich et al., 2019; Dalghi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 are widely expressed in tissues that respond to mechanical force.

claim: PIEZO2 expression in dorsal root ganglia sensory neurons is required for innocuous touch sensation.

claim: PIEZO2 expression in Merkel cells is required for innocuous touch sensation.

claim: PIEZO1 is highly expressed in mouse skin.
source: Because PIEZO1 is highly expressed in mouse skin (Coste et al., 2010), we hypothesized that this channel may be a key mechanotransducer in keratinocytes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of epidermal PIEZO1 decreases the firing rate of sensory nerve fibers in response to mechanical stimulation of the skin.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that loss of epidermal PIEZO1 decreases the firing rate of sensory nerve fibers in response to mechanical stimulation of the skin and blunts behavioral responses to both innocuous and noxious mechanical stimuli in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo tibial nerve recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of epidermal PIEZO1 blunts behavioral responses to innocuous mechanical stimuli in vivo.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that loss of epidermal PIEZO1 decreases the firing rate of sensory nerve fibers in response to mechanical stimulation of the skin and blunts behavioral responses to both innocuous and noxious mechanical stimuli in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of epidermal PIEZO1 blunts behavioral responses to noxious mechanical stimuli in vivo.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that loss of epidermal PIEZO1 decreases the firing rate of sensory nerve fibers in response to mechanical stimulation of the skin and blunts behavioral responses to both innocuous and noxious mechanical stimuli in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Epidermal PIEZO1 is critical for normal touch sensation.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that epidermal PIEZO1 is critical for normal touch sensation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Epidermal cell-specific PIEZO1 knockout mice (PIEZO1cKO) were generated by crossing Keratin14(Krt14)Cre and Piezo1loxp/loxp mice.
source: To determine if PIEZO1 is a mechanotransducer in keratinocytes, we generated epidermal cell-specific PIEZO1 knockout mice (PIEZO1cKO) by crossing Keratin14(Krt14)Cre and Piezo1loxp/loxp mice (Cahalan et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used to generate the knockout mice.

claim: RNA probes for Piezo1 stained the epidermis of wild-type mice.
source: RNA probes for Piezo1 stained the epidermis of wild-type mice, but Piezo1 puncta were absent from PIEZO1cKO epidermis (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Piezo1 puncta were absent from PIEZO1cKO epidermis.
source: RNA probes for Piezo1 stained the epidermis of wild-type mice, but Piezo1 puncta were absent from PIEZO1cKO epidermis (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PIEZO1 deletion did not disrupt gross epidermal morphology.
source: Importantly, PIEZO1 deletion did not disrupt gross epidermal morphology, as the stratum corneum and stratum spinosum appeared similar in PIEZO1cKO and wild-type mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Piezo1 transcript was detected in the epidermis of wild-type mice.
source: Quantitative real-time PCR also confirmed successful knockout of the channel; Piezo1 transcript was detected in the epidermis of wild-type mice but absent in PIEZO1cKO samples (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Piezo1 transcript was absent in PIEZO1cKO samples.
source: Quantitative real-time PCR also confirmed successful knockout of the channel; Piezo1 transcript was detected in the epidermis of wild-type mice but absent in PIEZO1cKO samples (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Keratinocytes isolated from wild-type animals responded robustly to Yoda1 in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: On a functional level, in vitro calcium imaging experiments revealed that keratinocytes isolated from wild-type animals responded robustly to the PIEZO1-specific chemical agonist Yoda1 (Syeda et al., 2015) in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Yoda1 is a PIEZO1-specific chemical agonist.
source: On a functional level, in vitro calcium imaging experiments revealed that keratinocytes isolated from wild-type animals responded robustly to the PIEZO1-specific chemical agonist Yoda1 (Syeda et al., 2015) in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Keratinocytes from PIEZO1cKO animals were virtually unresponsive to Yoda1.
source: In contrast, keratinocytes from PIEZO1cKO animals were virtually unresponsive to Yoda1 (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Primary human keratinocytes displayed robust, concentration-dependent intracellular calcium flux in response to Yoda1.
source: Similarly, primary human keratinocytes displayed robust, concentration-dependent intracellular calcium flux in response to Yoda1 (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Functional PIEZO1 is expressed in both human and mouse keratinocytes.
source: These data indicate that functional PIEZO1 is expressed in both human and mouse keratinocytes.
evidence: This is inferred from the Yoda1 calcium imaging experiments in both mouse and human keratinocytes.

claim: The majority of keratinocytes responded to a very gentle membrane indentation (≤1 µm) with a mechanically activated (MA) current.
source: Keratinocytes were sensitive to mechanical stimulation as the majority of cells responded to a very gentle membrane indentation (≤1 µm) with a mechanically activated (MA) current.
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp recordings described in the text.

claim: The amplitude of the MA current evoked by membrane indentation did not show a clear dependence on the increase in membrane indentation depth.
source: However, the amplitude of the MA current evoked by membrane indentation did not show a clear dependence on the increase in membrane indentation depth.
evidence: This is an observation from the patch clamp recordings.

claim: PIEZO1cKO keratinocytes required greater indentation to elicit MA currents compared to wild-type cells.
source: PIEZO1cKO keratinocytes required greater indentation to elicit MA currents compared to wild-type cells, indicating PIEZO1cKO keratinocytes have elevated mechanical thresholds (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PIEZO1cKO keratinocytes have elevated mechanical thresholds.
source: PIEZO1cKO keratinocytes required greater indentation to elicit MA currents compared to wild-type cells, indicating PIEZO1cKO keratinocytes have elevated mechanical thresholds (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PIEZO1cKO keratinocytes required greater indentation to elicit MA currents.

claim: There was an increase in the number of keratinocytes unresponsive to membrane indentation (mechanically insensitive) in the PIEZO1cKO group (51.35%, 19 out of 37 cells) compared to wild type group (21.74%, 5 out of 23 cells).
source: In addition, there was an increase in the number of keratinocytes unresponsive to membrane indentation (mechanically insensitive) in the PIEZO1cKO group (51.35%, 19 out of 37 cells) compared to wild type group (21.74%, 5 out of 23 cells) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was no change in the proportion of keratinocytes that responded to membrane indentation with rapidly adapting (RA), intermediately adapting (IA), or slowly adapting (SA) currents following PIEZO1 deletion.
source: However, there was no change in the proportion of keratinocytes that responded to membrane indentation with rapidly adapting (RA), intermediately adapting (IA), or slowly adapting (SA) currents (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: There was no change in the maximum current amplitude elicited by membrane indentation at any force tested following PIEZO1 deletion.
source: Furthermore, there was no change in the maximum current amplitude elicited by membrane indentation at any force tested (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: PIEZO1 is critical for setting the mechanical threshold of keratinocytes.
source: These findings indicate that PIEZO1 is critical for setting the mechanical threshold of keratinocytes and that its deletion increases the number of mechanically insensitive cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the patch clamp data showing elevated mechanical thresholds in PIEZO1cKO keratinocytes.

claim: PIEZO1 deletion increases the number of mechanically insensitive keratinocytes.
source: These findings indicate that PIEZO1 is critical for setting the mechanical threshold of keratinocytes and that its deletion increases the number of mechanically insensitive cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the patch clamp data showing more mechanically insensitive cells in PIEZO1cKO group.

claim: Keratinocytes modulate cutaneous sensory afferent responses to mechanical stimulation.
source: Since keratinocytes are known to modulate cutaneous sensory afferent responses to mechanical stimulation (Baumbauer et al., 2015), we next used ex vivo tibial nerve recordings to determine whether deletion of PIEZO1 in non-neuronal epidermal cells affects mechanically evoked sensory nerve firing.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to prior work.

claim: Aδ fibers from PIEZO1cKO mice fired fewer action potentials during mechanical stimulation of receptive fields than fibers isolated from wild-type control tissue.
source: Aδ fibers from PIEZO1cKO mice fired fewer action potentials during mechanical stimulation of receptive fields than fibers isolated from wild-type control tissue (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo tibial nerve recording data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The differences in Aδ fiber firing between PIEZO1cKO and wild-type mice were most notable at the upper range of tested forces (100-150mN).
source: These differences were most notable at the upper range of tested forces (100-150mN) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo tibial nerve recording data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Epidermal PIEZO1 knockout had no effect on the firing frequency of Aβ fibers.

claim: Epidermal PIEZO1 knockout had no effect on the firing frequency of C fibers.

evidence: This is supported by ex vivo tibial nerve recording data shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: No difference in mechanical thresholds between wild-type and PIEZO1cKO mice were observed for any fiber type.
source: No difference in mechanical thresholds between wild-type and PIEZO1cKO mice were observed for any fiber type (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D).

claim: The normal mechanically induced firing of Aδ primary afferent fibers depends on epidermal expression of PIEZO1.
source: Based on these data, the normal mechanically induced firing of Aδ primary afferent fibers depends on epidermal expression of PIEZO1.
evidence: This is inferred from the ex vivo tibial nerve recording data showing decreased Aδ fiber firing in PIEZO1cKO mice.

claim: Yoda1 induced dose-dependent paw attending responses in wild-type mice.
source: Yoda1 induced dose-dependent paw attending responses in wild-type mice (Figure 4A) but had no effect in PIEZO1cKO mice (Figure 4B), suggesting that the observed attending behaviors were dependent on epidermally-expressed PIEZO1.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Yoda1 had no effect on paw attending responses in PIEZO1cKO mice.
source: Yoda1 induced dose-dependent paw attending responses in wild-type mice (Figure 4A) but had no effect in PIEZO1cKO mice (Figure 4B), suggesting that the observed attending behaviors were dependent on epidermally-expressed PIEZO1.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Yoda1-induced attending behaviors were dependent on epidermally-expressed PIEZO1.
source: Yoda1 induced dose-dependent paw attending responses in wild-type mice (Figure 4A) but had no effect in PIEZO1cKO mice (Figure 4B), suggesting that the observed attending behaviors were dependent on epidermally-expressed PIEZO1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Yoda1 induced behaviors in wild-type but not PIEZO1cKO mice.

claim: Application of 1 mM Yoda1 failed to induce firing in any fiber type tested (Aβ, Aδ, C fibers).
source: To determine if these behaviors directly result from Yoda1-induced firing of sensory neurons, we performed ex vivo teased tibial nerve recordings in tissue isolated from wild-type mice. Application of 1 mM Yoda1 failed to induce firing in any fiber type tested (Aβ n=10, Aδ n=10, C n=10 fibers, data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: Yoda1 application increased the mechanically induced firing frequency of wild-type C fibers relative to vehicle application.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we found that Yoda1 application increased the mechanically induced firing frequency of wild-type C fibers relative to vehicle application (Figure 4C–F), but had no effect on the mechanically induced firing of Aβ or Aδ fibers (10 fibers of each tested, data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo tibial nerve recording data shown in Figure 4C-F.

claim: Yoda1 had no effect on the mechanically induced firing of Aβ fibers.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we found that Yoda1 application increased the mechanically induced firing frequency of wild-type C fibers relative to vehicle application (Figure 4C–F), but had no effect on the mechanically induced firing of Aβ or Aδ fibers (10 fibers of each tested, data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: Yoda1 had no effect on the mechanically induced firing of Aδ fibers.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we found that Yoda1 application increased the mechanically induced firing frequency of wild-type C fibers relative to vehicle application (Figure 4C–F), but had no effect on the mechanically induced firing of Aβ or Aδ fibers (10 fibers of each tested, data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: The increase in C fiber mechanically induced firing frequency following Yoda1 application was absent in PIEZO1cKO preparations.
source: The increase in C fiber mechanically induced firing frequency was absent in PIEZO1cKO preparations, indicating that epidermal PIEZO1 is required for the Yoda1-induced mechanical sensitization.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo tibial nerve recording data comparing wild-type and PIEZO1cKO preparations.

claim: Epidermal PIEZO1 is required for the Yoda1-induced mechanical sensitization.
source: The increase in C fiber mechanically induced firing frequency was absent in PIEZO1cKO preparations, indicating that epidermal PIEZO1 is required for the Yoda1-induced mechanical sensitization.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Yoda1-induced mechanical sensitization was absent in PIEZO1cKO preparations.

claim: Intraplantar injection of 1 mM Yoda1 sensitized wild-type mice behaviors to mechanical stimulation 30 minutes following injection.
source: Furthermore, we found that intraplantar injection of 1 mM Yoda1 sensitized wild-type mice behaviors to mechanical stimulation 30 minutes following injection, an effect which was absent in the PIEZO1ckO mice (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The Yoda1-induced mechanical sensitization was absent in PIEZO1cKO mice.
source: Furthermore, we found that intraplantar injection of 1 mM Yoda1 sensitized wild-type mice behaviors to mechanical stimulation 30 minutes following injection, an effect which was absent in the PIEZO1ckO mice (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Yoda1 acts at keratinocyte PIEZO1 to induce C fiber mechanical hypersensitivity that results in attending behaviors and increased mechanical sensitivity.
source: These results indicate that Yoda1 acts at keratinocyte PIEZO1 to induce C fiber mechanical hypersensitivity that results in attending behaviors and increased mechanical sensitivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of the Yoda1 experiments showing effects on C fiber firing and behavior that are dependent on epidermal PIEZO1.

claim: PIEZO1cKO mice were less sensitive to innocuous punctate stimulation with von Frey filaments.
source: PIEZO1cKO mice were less sensitive to innocuous punctate stimulation with von Frey filaments (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: PIEZO1cKO mice responded less frequently to paintbrush stimulation than wild-type controls.
source: Additionally, the response profiles to a dynamic light touch stimulus (paintbrush) and a noxious punctate (needle) stimulus were altered in PIEZO1cKO mice; PIEZO1cKO mice responded less frequently to both paintbrush and needle stimulation than wild-type controls (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: PIEZO1cKO mice responded less frequently to needle stimulation than wild-type controls.
source: Additionally, the response profiles to a dynamic light touch stimulus (paintbrush) and a noxious punctate (needle) stimulus were altered in PIEZO1cKO mice; PIEZO1cKO mice responded less frequently to both paintbrush and needle stimulation than wild-type controls (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: PIEZO1cKO mice did not exhibit general somatosensory deficits.
source: PIEZO1cKO mice did not exhibit general somatosensory deficits, as animal responses to heat (Figure 5F) and cold (Figure 5G) were identical to those observed in wild-type mice.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing no differences in heat and cold responses shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: Animal responses to heat were identical between PIEZO1cKO and wild-type mice.
source: PIEZO1cKO mice did not exhibit general somatosensory deficits, as animal responses to heat (Figure 5F) and cold (Figure 5G) were identical to those observed in wild-type mice.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Animal responses to cold were identical between PIEZO1cKO and wild-type mice.
source: PIEZO1cKO mice did not exhibit general somatosensory deficits, as animal responses to heat (Figure 5F) and cold (Figure 5G) were identical to those observed in wild-type mice.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Fewer PIEZO1cKO animals responded to the 0.6 g von Frey filament compared to wild-type animals.
source: PIEZO1cKO mice were less sensitive to stimulation with von Frey filaments; fewer PIEZO1cKO animals responded to the 0.6 g filament (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by high-speed imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PIEZO1cKO mice exhibited decreased mechanical sensitivity scores compared to wild-type animals.
source: PIEZO1cKO mice exhibited decreased mechanical sensitivity scores compared to wild-type animals, an effect that was most apparent in the needle stimulus (Figure 5H and I).
evidence: This is supported by high-speed imaging data shown in Figure 5H and I.

claim: The decrease in mechanical sensitivity scores in PIEZO1cKO mice was most apparent in the needle stimulus.

evidence: This is supported by high-speed imaging data shown in Figure 5H and I.

claim: PIEZO1 is one of the critical mechanotransducers in keratinocytes that enables these cells to encode mechanical force and convey this signal to sensory afferent terminals.
source: Here, we show for the first time that PIEZO1 is one of the critical mechanotransducers in keratinocytes that enables these cells to encode mechanical force and convey this signal to sensory afferent terminals.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the combined experimental data.

claim: These findings are the first to demonstrate a role for PIEZO1 in tactile sensation.
source: Our findings are the first to demonstrate a role for PIEZO1 in tactile sensation.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding of the study.

claim: PIEZO1 is necessary as a sensor of mechanical forces in the lung, bladder, and circulatory system.
source: These data complement previous work showing the necessity of this channel as a sensor of mechanical forces in the lung, bladder, and circulatory system (Li et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014a; Friedrich et al., 2019; Dalghi et al., 2019), and the necessity of family member PIEZO2 in the detection of light touch (Maksimovic et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2014; Hoffman et al., 2018; Ranade et al., 2014b; Chesler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: PIEZO2 is necessary for the detection of light touch.
source: These data complement previous work showing the necessity of this channel as a sensor of mechanical forces in the lung, bladder, and circulatory system (Li et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014a; Friedrich et al., 2019; Dalghi et al., 2019), and the necessity of family member PIEZO2 in the detection of light touch (Maksimovic et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2014; Hoffman et al., 2018; Ranade et al., 2014b; Chesler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: PIEZO1 regulates epidermal cell extrusion.
source: Furthermore, these results indicate that the functional contributions of PIEZO1 activity in the epidermis are multifaceted, as PIEZO1 also regulates epidermal cell extrusion and wound healing (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Holt et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: PIEZO1 regulates wound healing.
source: Furthermore, these results indicate that the functional contributions of PIEZO1 activity in the epidermis are multifaceted, as PIEZO1 also regulates epidermal cell extrusion and wound healing (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Holt et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Epidermal PIEZO1 deletion decreased animal behavioral responsiveness to a range of intensities and qualities of mechanical stimuli.
source: Epidermal PIEZO1 deletion decreased animal behavioral responsiveness to a range of intensities and qualities of mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Animals are not able to detect very light punctate stimuli when PIEZO2 is deleted from Merkel cells.
source: This contrasts to the behaviors observed when PIEZO2 is deleted from various peripheral cell types; animals are not able to detect very light punctate stimuli when PIEZO2 is deleted from Merkel cells (Maksimovic et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2014), and similarly, deletion of PIEZO2 from dorsal root ganglion neurons results in behavioral deficits to light punctate and dynamic stimuli but not to stimuli in the high to noxious range of forces (Ranade et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Deletion of PIEZO2 from dorsal root ganglion neurons results in behavioral deficits to light punctate and dynamic stimuli but not to stimuli in the high to noxious range of forces.
source: This contrasts to the behaviors observed when PIEZO2 is deleted from various peripheral cell types; animals are not able to detect very light punctate stimuli when PIEZO2 is deleted from Merkel cells (Maksimovic et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2014), and similarly, deletion of PIEZO2 from dorsal root ganglion neurons results in behavioral deficits to light punctate and dynamic stimuli but not to stimuli in the high to noxious range of forces (Ranade et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Merkel cell and neuronal PIEZO2 specifically mediate sensitivity to light touch.
source: While Merkel cell and neuronal PIEZO2 specifically mediate sensitivity to light touch, epidermal PIEZO1 appears to be a more general amplifier of cutaneous mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of PIEZO2 and PIEZO1 deletion phenotypes.

claim: Epidermal PIEZO1 appears to be a more general amplifier of cutaneous mechanical stimuli.
source: While Merkel cell and neuronal PIEZO2 specifically mediate sensitivity to light touch, epidermal PIEZO1 appears to be a more general amplifier of cutaneous mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that epidermal PIEZO1 deletion affects responses to a range of mechanical stimuli.

claim: Sensory neurons are capable of detecting and encoding aspects of mechanical stimuli without input from epidermal cells.
source: It is important to note that sensory neurons are capable of detecting and encoding aspects of mechanical stimuli without input from epidermal cells; neither epidermal PIEZO1 deletion nor optogenetic inhibition of keratinocytes completely abolishes touch sensation (Baumbauer et al., 2015; Moehring et al., 2018a), but rather both manipulations decrease neuronal and behavioral mechanical sensitivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that touch sensation is not completely abolished by epidermal PIEZO1 deletion or keratinocyte inhibition.

claim: Neither epidermal PIEZO1 deletion nor optogenetic inhibition of keratinocytes completely abolishes touch sensation.
source: It is important to note that sensory neurons are capable of detecting and encoding aspects of mechanical stimuli without input from epidermal cells; neither epidermal PIEZO1 deletion nor optogenetic inhibition of keratinocytes completely abolishes touch sensation (Baumbauer et al., 2015; Moehring et al., 2018a), but rather both manipulations decrease neuronal and behavioral mechanical sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by the current study's data and citations to prior work.

claim: Epidermal PIEZO1 deletion decreases neuronal mechanical sensitivity.
source: It is important to note that sensory neurons are capable of detecting and encoding aspects of mechanical stimuli without input from epidermal cells; neither epidermal PIEZO1 deletion nor optogenetic inhibition of keratinocytes completely abolishes touch sensation (Baumbauer et al., 2015; Moehring et al., 2018a), but rather both manipulations decrease neuronal and behavioral mechanical sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by the ex vivo tibial nerve recording data.

claim: Epidermal PIEZO1 deletion decreases behavioral mechanical sensitivity.
source: It is important to note that sensory neurons are capable of detecting and encoding aspects of mechanical stimuli without input from epidermal cells; neither epidermal PIEZO1 deletion nor optogenetic inhibition of keratinocytes completely abolishes touch sensation (Baumbauer et al., 2015; Moehring et al., 2018a), but rather both manipulations decrease neuronal and behavioral mechanical sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral assay data.

claim: Keratinocyte activation and subsequent signaling appears to function in concert with sensory neurons and other cutaneous end organ structures to amplify normal touch sensation.
source: Keratinocyte activation and subsequent signaling appears to function in concert with sensory neurons and other cutaneous end organ structures to amplify normal touch sensation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that keratinocyte PIEZO1 deletion decreases but does not abolish touch sensation.

claim: Keratinocytes are inherently mechanically sensitive.
source: Previous work has demonstrated that keratinocytes are inherently mechanically sensitive (Tsutsumi et al., 2009; Goto et al., 2010; Koizumi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: 51.35% of keratinocytes were insensitive to mechanical indentation following deletion of PIEZO1.
source: Here, we show that PIEZO1 deletion substantially reduces the number of keratinocytes that respond to membrane indentation; 51.35% of keratinocytes were insensitive to mechanical indentation following deletion of PIEZO1.
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp data.

claim: PIEZO2 mediates the rapidly adapting mechanical currents in DRG neurons and Merkel cells.
source: One potential candidate for this function is PIEZO2, which is shown to mediate the rapidly adapting mechanical currents in DRG neurons and Merkel cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Keratinocytes express low levels of PIEZO2 transcript.
source: However, keratinocytes express low levels of PIEZO2 transcript, making it unlikely to be the primary contributor to the remaining keratinocyte mechanical sensitivity (Hoffman et al., 2018; Coste et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Keratinocytes express members of the transient receptor potential (TRP) family of ion channels, such as TRPV4 and TRPC5.
source: In addition to PIEZO1, keratinocytes express a host of ion channels that may modulate keratinocyte mechanical responses downstream of bona fide mechanotransducers. These include members of the transient receptor potential (TRP) family of ion channels, such as TRPV4 and TRPC5 (Peier et al., 2002; Tu et al., 2005; O'Neil and Heller, 2005; Shen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: TRPV4 expression in keratinocytes is required for the development of mechanical allodynia in a mouse model of sunburn pain.
source: Interestingly, TRPV4 expression in keratinocytes is required for the development of mechanical allodynia in a mouse model of sunburn pain (Moore et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: TRPC5 expression is required for the development of mechanical allodynia in several inflammatory and neuropathic pain models.
source: Additionally, TRPC5 expression is required for the development of mechanical allodynia in several inflammatory and neuropathic pain models (Sadler et al., 2021), although the contribution of epidermal TRPC5 to injury induced mechanical hypersensitivity remains to be explored.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Deletion of PIEZO1 from the epidermis selectively decreased the firing frequency of Aδ fibers.
source: Our teased fiber recordings revealed that deletion of PIEZO1 from the epidermis selectively decreased the firing frequency of Aδ fibers.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo tibial nerve recording data.

claim: Epidermal PIEZO1 is important for the high intensity firing of Aδ fibers.
source: This difference was most notable at the higher range of forces tested, indicating that epidermal PIEZO1 is important for the high intensity firing of Aδ fibers.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the difference in Aδ fiber firing was most notable at higher forces.

claim: Aδ nociceptors mediate behavioral responses to pinprick stimuli.
source: Interestingly, Aδ nociceptors have been shown to mediate behavioral responses to pinprick stimuli (Arcourt et al., 2017), which was the behavior most affected by loss of epidermal PIEZO1 in our high-speed imaging experiments.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Epidermal PIEZO1 deletion had no effect on the mechanical responses of SA-Aβ fibers.
source: We found that epidermal PIEZO1 deletion had no effect on the mechanical responses of SA-Aβ fibers.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo tibial nerve recording data.

claim: Merkel cells tune the mechanical responses of SA-Aβ fibers.
source: This is likely because Merkel cells tune the mechanical responses of these fibers and Merkel cell mechanical sensitivity is primarily mediated by PIEZO2 (Maksimovic et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Merkel cell mechanical sensitivity is primarily mediated by PIEZO2.
source: This is likely because Merkel cells tune the mechanical responses of these fibers and Merkel cell mechanical sensitivity is primarily mediated by PIEZO2 (Maksimovic et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: C fiber afferents from PIEZO1cKO and wild-type preparations exhibited similar mechanical firing frequency.
source: Surprising to us, however, was that C fiber afferents from PIEZO1cKO and wild-type preparations exhibited similar mechanical firing frequency and mechanical thresholds.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo tibial nerve recording data.

claim: C fiber afferents from PIEZO1cKO and wild-type preparations exhibited similar mechanical thresholds.
source: Surprising to us, however, was that C fiber afferents from PIEZO1cKO and wild-type preparations exhibited similar mechanical firing frequency and mechanical thresholds.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo tibial nerve recording data.

claim: Many C fiber terminals are closely apposed to keratinocytes.
source: This was unexpected since many C fiber terminals are closely apposed to keratinocytes (Zylka et al., 2005) and, in experiments performed by Baumbauer, Deberry, and Adelman, et al., optogenetic inhibition of epidermal cells decreased C fiber mechanical firing in 12 of 25 fibers tested (Baumbauer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of epidermal cells decreased C fiber mechanical firing in 12 of 25 fibers tested.
source: This was unexpected since many C fiber terminals are closely apposed to keratinocytes (Zylka et al., 2005) and, in experiments performed by Baumbauer, Deberry, and Adelman, et al., optogenetic inhibition of epidermal cells decreased C fiber mechanical firing in 12 of 25 fibers tested (Baumbauer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Many C fibers terminate more superficially in the epidermis than Aδ fibers.
source: Alternatively, because many C fibers terminate more superficially in the epidermis than Aδ fibers (Zylka et al., 2005), it is possible that the differentiated keratinocytes of the outer epidermis rely on a different mechanotransducer than PIEZO1 to encode tactile information.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Keratinocytes release ATP in response to mechanical stimulation.
source: We recently reported that keratinocytes release ATP in response to mechanical stimulation, which subsequently acts at purinergic receptors on sensory terminals to mediate tactile sensation (Moehring et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: ATP acts at purinergic receptors on sensory terminals to mediate tactile sensation.
source: We recently reported that keratinocytes release ATP in response to mechanical stimulation, which subsequently acts at purinergic receptors on sensory terminals to mediate tactile sensation (Moehring et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: ATP may be one of the signaling molecules linking epidermal PIEZO1 activity to sensory neuron responses.
source: Therefore, ATP may be one of the signaling molecules linking epidermal PIEZO1 activity to sensory neuron responses.
evidence: This is speculated based on prior work showing keratinocytes release ATP in response to mechanical stimulation.

claim: Keratinocytes can release calcitonin gene-related peptide β, acetylcholine, glutamate, epinephrine, neurotrophic growth factors, endothelin-1, and cytokines.
source: In addition to ATP, keratinocytes can release a variety of other neuroactive factors, including calcitonin gene-related peptide β, acetylcholine, glutamate, epinephrine, neurotrophic growth factors, endothelin-1, and cytokines (Hou et al., 2011; Shi et al., 2013; Barr et al., 2013; Moore et al., 2013; Lumpkin and Caterina, 2007) the contribution of these ligands to neuro-epithelial mechanical signaling remains to be explored.
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Merkel cells express K14.
source: For example, Merkel cells express K14 and would have PIEZO1 deleted from them (Maksimovic et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Merkel cells express minimal PIEZO1.
source: However, given that keratinocytes make up the vast majority of cells in the epidermis (>95%) (Fuchs, 1995), and Merkel cells express minimal PIEZO1 (Maksimovic et al., 2014; Hoffman et al., 2018), we hypothesize that our findings are largely mediated by keratinocytes.
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Sensory Schwann cells do not express Keratin 14.
source: Furthermore, it is unlikely that our PIEZO1 deletion is targeting the recently discovered sensory Schwann cells, as these cells do not express Keratin 14 (P. Ernfors, personal communication, unpublished data).
evidence: This is stated based on personal communication with another researcher.

claim: Yoda1 application induced robust calcium flux in isolated mouse keratinocytes.
source: Yoda1 application induced robust calcium flux in both isolated mouse and human keratinocytes.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: Yoda1 application induced robust calcium flux in isolated human keratinocytes.
source: Yoda1 application induced robust calcium flux in both isolated mouse and human keratinocytes.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: The functional expression of PIEZO1 in human keratinocytes suggests that epidermal PIEZO1 may play a role in human touch sensation.
source: The functional expression of PIEZO1 in human keratinocytes is intriguing as it suggests that epidermal PIEZO1 may also play a role in human touch sensation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that human keratinocytes express functional PIEZO1.

claim: PIEZO1 loss of function mutations have been identified in human patients.
source: PIEZO1 loss of function mutations have been identified in human patients (Lukacs et al., 2015; Alper, 2017), but to our knowledge, quantitative sensory testing, like that which has been performed in patients with PIEZO2 loss of function mutations (Chesler et al., 2016), has not yet been completed in these individuals.
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Quantitative sensory testing has been performed in patients with PIEZO2 loss of function mutations.
source: PIEZO1 loss of function mutations have been identified in human patients (Lukacs et al., 2015; Alper, 2017), but to our knowledge, quantitative sensory testing, like that which has been performed in patients with PIEZO2 loss of function mutations (Chesler et al., 2016), has not yet been completed in these individuals.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Intraplantar injection of Yoda1 induced paw attending behaviors in wild-type mice.
source: We found that intraplantar injection of the PIEZO1 specific agonist Yoda1 induced paw attending behaviors in wild-type but not PIEZO1cKO mice, suggesting that activation of epidermal PIEZO1 is sufficient to induce behavioral responses.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data.

claim: Intraplantar injection of Yoda1 did not induce paw attending behaviors in PIEZO1cKO mice.
source: We found that intraplantar injection of the PIEZO1 specific agonist Yoda1 induced paw attending behaviors in wild-type but not PIEZO1cKO mice, suggesting that activation of epidermal PIEZO1 is sufficient to induce behavioral responses.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data.

claim: Activation of epidermal PIEZO1 is sufficient to induce behavioral responses.
source: We found that intraplantar injection of the PIEZO1 specific agonist Yoda1 induced paw attending behaviors in wild-type but not PIEZO1cKO mice, suggesting that activation of epidermal PIEZO1 is sufficient to induce behavioral responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Yoda1 induced behaviors in wild-type but not PIEZO1cKO mice.

claim: PIEZO1 is functionally expressed in itch-specific sensory neurons.
source: This result was surprising given that Yoda1 induced calcium responses in isolated keratinocytes and PIEZO1 is functionally expressed in itch-specific sensory neurons (Hill et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Yoda1 can activate PIEZO1 channels on its own.
source: Indeed, while Yoda1 can activate PIEZO1 channels on its own, it prominently sensitizes PIEZO1 to mechanical stimulation (Syeda et al., 2015; Lacroix et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Yoda1 prominently sensitizes PIEZO1 to mechanical stimulation.
source: Indeed, while Yoda1 can activate PIEZO1 channels on its own, it prominently sensitizes PIEZO1 to mechanical stimulation (Syeda et al., 2015; Lacroix et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Subthreshold mechanical stimulation could induce firing in high-threshold mechanically sensitive afferents when paired with optogenetic activation of keratinocytes.
source: Interestingly, the team of Baumbauer, DeBerry, and Adelman reported that subthreshold mechanical stimulation could induce firing in high-threshold mechanically sensitive afferents when paired with optogenetic activation of keratinocytes (Baumbauer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Sensitization of keratinocyte mechanical signaling may enhance sensory afferent responses to force.
source: This suggests that sensitization of keratinocyte mechanical signaling may enhance sensory afferent responses to force.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that optogenetic activation of keratinocytes can induce firing in afferents with subthreshold mechanical stimulation.

claim: Injury induced sensitization of keratinocyte mechanotransduction may contribute to the development of mechanical allodynia and hyperalgesia.
source: This idea is intriguing, as injury induced sensitization of keratinocyte mechanotransduction may contribute to the development of mechanical allodynia and hyperalgesia.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that keratinocyte signaling can enhance sensory afferent responses.

claim: Alterations in keratinocyte function and signaling contribute to inflammatory and neuropathic cutaneous pain states.
source: Alterations in keratinocyte function and signaling contribute to inflammatory and neuropathic cutaneous pain states, such as psoriasis, dermatitis, fibromyalgia, complex regional pain syndrome, and postherpetic neuralgia (Benhadou et al., 2019; Kim and Leung, 2018; Li et al., 2009; Evdokimov et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: UVB light exposure resulted in profound mechanical and heat allodynia in a mouse model of sunburn pain.
source: Furthermore, in a mouse model of sunburn pain, UVB light exposure resulted in profound mechanical and heat allodynia, effects which were completely dependent on UVB-induced activation and sensitization of keratinocyte expressed TRPV4 (Moore et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: UVB-induced mechanical and heat allodynia were completely dependent on UVB-induced activation and sensitization of keratinocyte expressed TRPV4.
source: Furthermore, in a mouse model of sunburn pain, UVB light exposure resulted in profound mechanical and heat allodynia, effects which were completely dependent on UVB-induced activation and sensitization of keratinocyte expressed TRPV4 (Moore et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Injury-induced sensitization of keratinocyte mechanotransducers may enhance normal keratinocyte activation in response to mechanical stimulation and subsequent signaling to sensory neurons.
source: Thus, injury-induced sensitization of keratinocyte mechanotransducers may enhance normal keratinocyte activation in response to mechanical stimulation and subsequent signaling to sensory neurons.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that keratinocyte TRPV4 sensitization contributes to sunburn pain.

claim: Epidermal PIEZO1 is critical for normal touch sensation in mice.
source: In summary, the data presented here demonstrate that epidermal PIEZO1 is critical for normal touch sensation in mice and that PIEZO1 is also expressed and functional in human keratinocytes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the combined experimental data.

claim: PIEZO1 is expressed and functional in human keratinocytes.
source: In summary, the data presented here demonstrate that epidermal PIEZO1 is critical for normal touch sensation in mice and that PIEZO1 is also expressed and functional in human keratinocytes.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data from human keratinocytes.

claim: Keratin 14 is expressed in all keratinocytes as early as E9.5.
source: To target epidermal keratinocytes, a Keratin14 (Krt14)Cre driver was used, as Krt14 is expressed in all keratinocytes as early as E9.5 (Byrne et al., 1994; Wang et al., 1997; Dassule et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Male and female mice were analyzed separately, and no sex differences were observed.
source: Male and female mice were analyzed separately, and no sex differences were observed.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Virtually all keratinocytes isolated from mouse skin respond to the PIEZO1 agonist Yoda1.
source: Here, we show that virtually all keratinocytes isolated from mouse and human skin respond to the PIEZO1 agonist Yoda1 and that PIEZO1 expression is important for keratinocyte mechanical sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing high percentage of responding cells.

claim: Virtually all keratinocytes isolated from human skin respond to the PIEZO1 agonist Yoda1.
source: Here, we show that virtually all keratinocytes isolated from mouse and human skin respond to the PIEZO1 agonist Yoda1 and that PIEZO1 expression is important for keratinocyte mechanical sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing high percentage of responding cells.

claim: PIEZO1 expression is important for keratinocyte mechanical sensitivity.
source: Here, we show that virtually all keratinocytes isolated from mouse and human skin respond to the PIEZO1 agonist Yoda1 and that PIEZO1 expression is important for keratinocyte mechanical sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp data showing elevated mechanical thresholds and increased mechanically insensitive cells in PIEZO1cKO keratinocytes.
